title: Leaning in to Stop the Spread
summary: For 24 years, Under Armour has pushed the limits of the world of sports performance with product innovations developed to make all athletes better. Last week, the brand began putting that experience to work helping health care systems defend against the coronavirus pandemic. To support the University of Maryland Medical System’s (UMMS) 28,000 health care providers and staff, Under Armour has begun to manufacture and assemble face masks, face shields and specially equipped fanny packs, and is also exploring fabricating hospital gowns for the statewide medical system. The brand will also begin providing face masks to LifeBridge, a regional health care organization based in Baltimore. Additionally, Under Armour is currently discussing the needs for supplies with Johns Hopkins Medicine, MedStar and other local medical institutions. "When the call came in from our local medical providers for more masks, gowns and supply kits, we just went straight to work," said Randy Harward, SVP of Advanced Material and Manufacturing Innovation at Under Armour. “More than 50 Under Armour teammates from materials scientists to footwear and apparel designers from laboratories in Baltimore and Portland quickly came together in search of solutions.”

title: The Energy Needed to Power the IoT Revolution Is All Around Us
summary: The IoT revolution will rely on sensors spread across extremely large and remote areas, and powering them will require innovative solutions.
body_text: Batteries The problem of providing electricity to low-power IoT devices seems like it should be able to be solved with the same technology that power most of the wireless devices we use every day, batteries. This is a fine solution for some low-power devices, it’s relatively cheap and the technology is tried-and-true. It’s an especially suitable solution if the nodes are easily accessible and their batteries are simple to replace. However, in situations where the edge device is not easily accessible—perhaps it’s a soil moisture sensor buried in a field or an industrial sensor secreted away behind hard-to-move machinery—batteries might not be the ideal solution, even if they can last for years in some situations. This is especially true in large deployments, where replacing batteries could turn into a never-ending game of whack-a-mole—a very expensive one at that. Batteries are certainly the most familiar technology on this list, but there are several more long-lasting alternatives that could prove promising. Solar Solar power is another IoT energy option with which most of us are already familiar. In areas where conditions are right, solar panels could provide power to single devices or clusters of devices. Of course, indoor deployments or those in areas that are perpetually in shadow would not be good candidates for the technology. When paired with a rechargeable battery, these devices could operate independently for sustained periods. Solar power is also a proven technology, and photovoltaic cells have only been getting cheaper and more efficient with time. Of the energy harvesting options presented in this list, solar is capable of producing the most power. However, there are other zero-power technologies being developed for IoT applications that take more novel approaches to powering nodes. Thermoelectric This form of energy harvesting uses the properties of thermoelectric materials to produce electricity when there is a variation in temperature across the material (i.e., when one side is hotter than the other). This is another power solution that works extremely well in conjunction with machinery, as it often produces quite a bit of heat waste. Because these thermoelectric generators don’t have moving parts, they can operate for extremely long periods without needing to be replaced. Some wearable tech companies are even looking at incorporating thermoelectric generators into clothing, using the wearer’s own body heat to produce electricity. (Insert your own The Matrix joke here.) Vibrational Factories and farms are busy places full of humming machinery and rumbling vehicles. Fortunately, all this kinetic energy can be transformed into electrical energy via a process called vibrational energy harvesting. This technique uses magnetic induction to transform a moving magnetic field into electromotive force. Essentially, as long as the edge device is moving, it will be able to generate power. This is great for sensors that operate on machinery or vehicles because the vibrations they produce have a consistent direction and frequency. But don’t count out other clever applications; vibrational energy harvesting could crop up in many unexpected places. In fact, the technology is being used to power sensors on buoys at sea, using the motion of the buoys bobbing up and down on the waves to produce enough energy to power the devices. RF Harvesting Of all the solutions we have delved into, this is the most fanciful, allowing a device to seemingly pull power from the very air around it. In actuality, the device uses a receiving antenna to pick up ambient radio frequency (RF) signals, which it then converts into energy. So where do these RF signals come from? Well, luckily, they’re already all around us. RF signals are given off by sources including radio and TV transmitters, Wi-Fi routers, the GSM system (3G, 4G, 5G, etc.), satellite stations, and radar. Dense urban centers have plenty of sources of ambient RF to draw power from, but even in rural environments, agricultural operations could use RF transmitters to energize their hard-to-reach devices. In fact, the long-range, low-power LoRaWan network already uses RF signals to communicate with edge devices, meaning all of its nodes will have access to some RF source that could potentially be used for power. They are impressively efficient too, with modern designs capable of converting more than 50 percent of the energy they are able to capture into usable current, making it an exciting, green source of energy to power the IoT revolution. However, that efficiency belies the main trouble with RF harvesting: signal strength. Propagation loss leads to large drop-offs in signal strength as the distance from the node to the source increases and absorption loss takes a toll when the signal has to pass through obstacles, meaning the node ideally needs to be near the RF source without any objects in between to reduce the signal. Among the power sources we have discussed, RF harvesting is currently capable of providing enough energy for only the most extremely low-power devices—though the method should become more feasible with time as technology improves and new sources of RF signals are brought online.

title: Las micro decisiones que afectan tu crédito sin que te des cuenta
summary: ¿Buscas fortalecer tus hábitos financieros? Descubre cuáles son esas micro decisiones que afectan tu crédito.
body_text: ¡Ahora puedes solicitar tu crédito por whatsapp! Sin papeleos ni complicaciones Pídelo ahora El acceso a un crédito no depende únicamente de grandes decisiones financieras, sino también de pequeñas acciones cotidianas que, con el tiempo, reflejan la forma en que una persona administra su dinero. Hábitos como pagar a tiempo, registrar ingresos, usar medios de pago digitales y organizar los gastos contribuyen a construir ese perfil. Hoy, la estabilidad financiera no se mide solo por el nivel de ingresos, sino también por la disciplina, la organización y la constancia en el manejo de los recursos. Por ello, las llamadas micro decisiones financieras tienen un papel cada vez más relevante en la percepción del comportamiento económico. Más que una compra o una transacción aislada, lo que realmente influye son los patrones que se mantienen durante semanas, meses o años. La buena noticia es que cualquier persona puede fortalecer esos hábitos mediante pequeños cambios sostenidos, sin necesidad de realizar transformaciones drásticas ni contar con altos ingresos. En este artículo conocerás cuáles son esas micro decisiones que suelen pasar desapercibidas, cómo pueden influir en tu perfil financiero y qué estrategias puedes aplicar para fortalecer poco a poco la confianza que proyectas hacia el sistema financiero. Pequeñas acciones financieras que influyen en tu perfil económico Puede que te pase a ti. La mayoría de las personas toma decenas de decisiones relacionadas con el dinero cada semana sin ser plenamente consciente de ello. Muchas parecen insignificantes, pero juntas forman un patrón de comportamiento financiero. Algunos ejemplos son: Pagar los servicios públicos antes de la fecha límite. Registrar correctamente los ingresos recibidos. Revisar periódicamente los movimientos bancarios. Utilizar medios de pago digitales cuando sea posible. Evitar gastos impulsivos. Organizar los pagos del mes mediante un presupuesto. Ninguna de estas acciones garantiza por sí sola mejores oportunidades financieras. Sin embargo, cuando se convierten en hábitos constantes ayudan a reflejar organización y disciplina. También influyen aspectos como la manera de administrar el dinero disponible. Por ejemplo, una persona que conoce cuánto ingresa, cuánto gasta y cuánto puede ahorrar suele tomar decisiones más informadas que alguien que administra sus recursos de forma improvisada. Las pequeñas acciones repetidas construyen una historia financiera mucho más sólida que los esfuerzos ocasionales. La clave no está en hacer algo extraordinario una vez, sino en mantener buenos hábitos durante largos períodos. Cómo los hábitos diarios pueden impactar futuras oportunidades financieras Muchas oportunidades financieras no dependen únicamente del presente. Las entidades suelen analizar cómo ha sido el comportamiento económico de una persona a lo largo del tiempo. Por eso los hábitos diarios adquieren tanta importancia. Organización constante Llevar un control de ingresos y gastos permite comprender mejor la situación financiera personal. Esto facilita la toma de decisiones responsables. Puntualidad en los compromisos Cumplir con las obligaciones económicas refleja responsabilidad financiera. La puntualidad continúa siendo uno de los hábitos más valorados dentro del sistema financiero. Actividad financiera organizada El uso frecuente y ordenado de herramientas financieras genera una mayor visibilidad de la actividad económica. Esto puede contribuir a construir un perfil financiero más completo. Planeación Las personas que planifican sus gastos suelen enfrentar con mayor facilidad los imprevistos financieros. La planeación reduce la necesidad de tomar decisiones impulsivas. Construcción gradual de confianza La confianza financiera no aparece de un día para otro. Se construye mediante cientos de pequeñas decisiones que demuestran consistencia en el manejo del dinero. Precisamente por eso resulta tan importante prestar atención a los hábitos cotidianos. Errores frecuentes que muchas personas pasan por alto No todos los errores financieros están relacionados con grandes deudas o inversiones equivocadas. En ocasiones son pequeños descuidos que, repetidos durante mucho tiempo, terminan afectando la organización financiera. No llevar un registro de gastos Muchas personas desconocen exactamente en qué utilizan su dinero cada mes. Esta falta de información dificulta la planeación financiera. Dejar todo para última hora Esto es típico de los colombianos. Esperar hasta el último momento para realizar pagos aumenta el riesgo de olvidos y retrasos. Depender exclusivamente del efectivo Aunque el efectivo sigue siendo un medio de pago válido, utilizar únicamente dinero físico puede dificultar el seguimiento de los movimientos financieros. No revisar periódicamente las cuentas Consultar con frecuencia los movimientos ayuda a detectar errores, identificar gastos innecesarios y mantener un mayor control financiero. Gastar sin un objetivo claro Cuando no existe un presupuesto o una planeación básica, resulta más fácil realizar compras impulsivas. Descuidar pequeños compromisos En ocasiones las personas prestan atención únicamente a las obligaciones más importantes y olvidan pagos menores que también requieren organización. Corregir estos hábitos suele ser mucho más sencillo de lo que parece y puede generar beneficios importantes con el paso del tiempo. Estrategias para fortalecer tu comportamiento financiero poco a poco Mejorar el perfil financiero no requiere cambios radicales. En la mayoría de los casos basta con incorporar pequeñas acciones que puedan mantenerse de forma constante. Elabora un presupuesto sencillo No es necesario utilizar herramientas complejas. Lo importante es conocer cuánto dinero ingresa y cómo se distribuyen los gastos. Programa recordatorios de pago Las aplicaciones móviles permiten recibir alertas para evitar olvidos. Utiliza herramientas digitales Aprende a conocer las plataformas financieras ya que estas facilitan el registro automático de movimientos y ayudan a mantener una mejor organización. Revisa tus movimientos cada semana Dedicar algunos minutos a revisar las transacciones permite identificar oportunidades de mejora. Define metas alcanzables Los objetivos pequeños suelen ser más fáciles de cumplir y ayudan a mantener la motivación. Mantén hábitos constantes La consistencia genera mejores resultados que los cambios temporales. Es preferible realizar pequeñas mejoras durante varios meses que intentar modificar todos los hábitos en pocos días. La importancia de la constancia en la construcción de confianza financiera La confianza financiera se construye principalmente a través de la constancia en hábitos responsables, más que por el nivel de ingresos. Acciones como pagar a tiempo, registrar gastos y administrar el dinero con planificación fortalecen una trayectoria financiera sólida con el paso del tiempo. Gracias a la transformación digital, muchas de estas acciones quedan registradas y pueden contribuir a una visión más completa del comportamiento financiero. En este contexto, MONET utiliza herramientas tecnológicas confiables para analizar la actividad financiera cotidiana y desarrollar evaluaciones más amplias, favoreciendo la inclusión financiera de personas con poca experiencia crediticia y promoviendo una cultura basada en la organización, la educación financiera y la disciplina. Y tú, ¿ya estás listo para mejorar las decisiones que afectan tu crédito? Preguntas frecuentes ¿Qué son las micro decisiones financieras? Son pequeñas acciones relacionadas con el manejo cotidiano del dinero, como organizar gastos, pagar oportunamente o registrar movimientos financieros. ¿Una sola decisión afecta mi acceso al crédito? Generalmente no. Lo que suele tener mayor relevancia es el conjunto de hábitos que una persona mantiene de forma constante a lo largo del tiempo. ¿Cómo puedo mejorar mi comportamiento financiero? Comenzando por acciones sencillas como elaborar un presupuesto, controlar los gastos, cumplir oportunamente las obligaciones y mantener una buena organización financiera. ¿Por qué la constancia es tan importante? Porque los hábitos repetidos reflejan disciplina y estabilidad, elementos que contribuyen a construir una trayectoria financiera más sólida. En conclusión: Las oportunidades financieras se construyen a partir de pequeños hábitos cotidianos, como organizar el presupuesto, registrar los gastos y cumplir con los pagos a tiempo. La constancia en estas acciones fortalece la estabilidad económica y refleja una buena administración de los recursos. La educación financiera se basa en desarrollar prácticas responsables de forma sostenida. body_text: Gaurav Munj 2022-03-04T06:42:16+00:00 Press Release Details Upcoming and Recent Events Corporate Presentation SEC Filings Stock Quote & Chart Historical Lookup Governance Documents Committees July 27, 2026 at 7:00 AM EDT Federal Jury Finds Avilar Therapeutics and RA Capital Willfully and Maliciously Misappropriated Trade Secret Developed at Yale, Awards Biohaven and Yale University $4 Million PDF Version NEW HAVEN, Conn. , July 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Biohaven Ltd. and/or its wholly owned subsidiaries ("Biohaven") (NYSE: BHVN) and Yale University ("Yale") today announced that a federal jury in the U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware returned a verdict in their favor in the trade secret misappropriation and breach of contract litigation against Avilar Therapeutics, Inc. ("Avilar") and RA Capital Management GP, LLC ("RA Capital"). The jury found that Avilar and RA Capital willfully and maliciously misappropriated a Yale trade secret relating to its "MODA" targeted protein degradation platform, and that RA Capital separately breached its 2019 confidentiality agreement with Yale. The jury awarded Yale and Biohaven a combined $4 million in damages — $2 million to Yale for RA Capital's breach of contract, and $1 million each to Yale and Biohaven for trade secret misappropriation. "This verdict confirms what we have said since we filed this case: RA Capital and Avilar improperly used confidential information to advance a competing company, and the jury agreed that they did so willfully and maliciously," said Dr. Vlad Coric, Chief Executive Officer of Biohaven. "We are grateful to the jury for paying careful attention to the evidence and to our legal team for their extraordinary work at trial. Biohaven is appreciative for our continued partnership with academic institutions like Yale, and remains committed to our mission of discovering, developing, and commercializing life-changing therapies for people with debilitating diseases." Karen Peart, Yale's Associate Vice President for Communications, added, "Dr. Spiegel's work is the product of years of novel and rigorous research on extracellular degraders at Yale and exemplifies the innovative scholarship Yale faculty have advanced for decades. Yale is committed to fostering an environment where groundbreaking discoveries can flourish, improving lives, driving economic growth, and strengthening America's competitiveness. Through collaborations with industry partners, the university helps ensure that promising discoveries can be translated efficiently into products and therapies that serve the public good. These relationships depend on trust, integrity, and respect for the legal obligations that enable universities and industry to work together to advance innovation." Biohaven was represented by K&L Gates LLP and Morris James LLP. Susman Godfrey LLP and Farnan LLP represented Yale. Background of the Case Dr. David Spiegel, a professor at Yale, developed the MODA platform, a technology designed to bind and eliminate disease-causing extracellular proteins from the body, and presented it at Yale's Lifesciences Pitchfest in 2018. RA Capital, a healthcare-focused investment firm, subsequently entered into a confidentiality agreement with Yale in April 2019 to evaluate a potential investment in and partnership around the technology. Over the following months, Dr. Spiegel shared confidential and detailed technical information with RA Capital, and the parties negotiated the terms of a possible deal. Those negotiations ended without an agreement in August 2019. Biohaven and Yale alleged that RA Capital, together with Avilar Therapeutics, a company RA Capital helped establish later that year, used confidential information from those discussions to build a competing drug development program instead of pursuing a partnership with Yale. Biohaven licensed the MODA platform from Yale to develop and commercialize the technology. Biohaven and Yale filed suit against Avilar and RA Capital in March 2023 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware, alleging trade secret misappropriation and breach of the confidentiality agreement between Yale and RA Capital. The case proceeded to a jury trial beginning July 20, 2026 and the jury returned its verdict on July 24, 2026. About Biohaven Biohaven Ltd. title: How Much Does Customer Feedback Analytics Software Actually Cost?
summary: Customer feedback analytics software costs $19/month to several hundred thousand per year. Real price bands, pricing models, and the hidden costs.
body_text: Anyone who has tried to budget for customer feedback analytics knows the frustration: almost every enterprise vendor's pricing page says "contact sales." The numbers that do exist online come from competitor blogs and procurement platforms, not from the vendors themselves. That makes it hard to know whether a quote is reasonable before you are three calls deep into a sales cycle. Here is the honest answer. Customer feedback analytics software spans three price bands: self-serve survey tools from roughly $19 to $50 per month, mid-market analytics platforms from roughly $25,000 per year, and enterprise platforms that typically run from tens of thousands to several hundred thousand dollars per year depending on data volume. Thematic, like most enterprise feedback analytics vendors, prices on usage: comment volume, the number of datasets, how each dataset is analyzed, and the support level, quoted as a custom proposal. The license is only part of the real number. Professional services, implementation, and overage charges can add 50% or more to what you actually spend. This article breaks down the three bands with verifiable numbers, explains the pricing models behind the quotes, itemizes the hidden costs, and ends with the questions that surface a vendor's real total cost before you sign. What "customer feedback analytics software" covers Customer feedback analytics software analyzes unstructured feedback (open-ended survey responses, support tickets, reviews, call transcripts) and turns it into themes, sentiment, and metrics teams can act on. It is a different purchase from survey software, even though the categories overlap at the low end. The distinction matters for budgeting: Survey tools collect feedback. Pricing is usually per user or per response, published openly, and cheap. Feedback analytics platforms analyze feedback from many sources. Pricing is usually based on data volume, and at the enterprise level it is almost always a custom quote. CX suites bundle collection, analytics, and workflow. Pricing combines platform tiers with usage and add-on fees. If a vendor publishes a low monthly price, you are almost certainly looking at a collection tool, not an analytics platform. The three price bands, with real numbers Band Typical price Examples with published or filed prices Self-serve survey tools $19 to $50 per month entry, scaling with users and responses SurveyMonkey from about $25 per user per month; SurveySparrow from about $19 per month; Zonka Feedback from about $49 per month Mid-market analytics platforms Roughly $25,000 to $75,000 per year SentiSum publishes pricing from $3,000 per month, based on channels and feedback volume; enterprise VoC commitments commonly start near $25,000 per year Enterprise feedback analytics and CX platforms Tens of thousands to several hundred thousand dollars per year Qualtrics deal data shows a median near $30,000 per year with contracts ranging past $126,000; Medallia's publicly filed government price schedule listed platform tiers from $20,000 to $168,000 per year Two reference points deserve special attention because they are unusually verifiable. Qualtrics transaction data. Procurement platform Vendr reports a median Qualtrics contract around $30,000 per year across 276 deals, with a range from about $6,500 to over $126,000. Averages skew much higher than medians in this market because a small number of very large contracts pull the mean up. When a vendor cites an "average customer," ask for the median instead. Medallia's filed government pricing. Medallia's public-sector price schedule (filed around 2021, so treat it as a dated reference point rather than current commercial pricing) listed platform tiers from $20,000 to $168,000 per year, and advanced feature tiers, including text analytics and AI add-ons, from $10,000 to $675,000 per year. The detail worth noticing: the analytics add-ons could cost more than the platform itself. That is what happens when text analytics is sold as a bolt-on to a suite rather than being the product. How enterprise pricing actually works Enterprise feedback analytics quotes are built from a small set of pricing models. Knowing which one you are in tells you how the cost will behave as your program grows. Per-interaction or per-record pricing. Qualtrics moved to interaction-based pricing in April 2024 : CX suites are billed by the volume of survey responses, calls, chats, emails, and social reviews processed, with unlimited users. Medallia prices on "Experience Data Records," a similar usage-based unit. The upside is that seats are free, so you can roll insights out widely. The risk is that cost scales directly with feedback volume: a platform priced for today's channels gets materially more expensive as you add sources. Volume-and-scope pricing. Thematic prices on comment volume, the number of datasets, how each dataset is analyzed, and the support level, quoted as a custom proposal . This is also usage-based, but scoped to analysis rather than to every interaction touched, and it comes with a specific TCO argument: theme discovery and maintenance happen in the product, so keeping the model current does not require a professional services engagement. Platform tiers plus add-ons. The suite model visible in Medallia's filed schedule: a platform tier sets the base, and capabilities like text analytics, AI features, and journey analytics are priced as separate add-on tiers. The quote looks modest until the add-ons that make the platform useful are included. The hidden costs that change the real number The license is the visible number. Three other line items decide the real one. Implementation and professional services. Reports on Medallia implementations describe 6 to 12 month timelines with $50,000 to $200,000 or more in services on top of the license. Medallia's own filed schedule listed professional services rates from roughly $110 to $392 per hour. Any platform that needs vendor services to configure taxonomies or build reports carries this cost for its whole life, not just at setup. Overages and escalation. Usage-priced platforms charge for volume above the contracted band. Analyses of Qualtrics contracts describe first-year hidden costs in the $8,000 to $10,000 range from implementation, overages, and add-ons, plus annual price escalation at renewal. Analyst time. The quietest cost is the one on your own payroll. A Forrester Total Economic Impact study commissioned by Thematic quantified it for a composite organization: $652,000 per year in savings from automating manual analysis, representing 4,250 hours of data preparation and the equivalent of two full-time analysts. If a cheaper tool leaves the coding and reporting work with your team, it is not cheaper. For teams weighing the do-it-yourself route instead, Thematic's build-cost analysis estimates an in-house AI feedback platform at roughly $1.8 million over five years, against roughly $900,000 over five years for a comparable SaaS deployment. The figures are illustrative, but the two-to-one ratio is the point. What the money buys: cost against outcomes A price is only high or low relative to what it returns. The verifiable outcomes in this category look like this. The Forrester TEI study of Thematic found a 543% return on investment over three years, with payback in under six months and insight delivery cut from weeks to minutes. Greyhound, the intercity bus network, reduced feedback analysis that took two to three weeks to ten minutes, and its NPS rose about 15 points within a few months. Community Health System, a not-for-profit healthcare network in California's central San Joaquin Valley, produced 250 one-page department reports from employee survey feedback in three days, saving 160+ hours and about $10,000 per reporting cycle. Atom Bank, the UK's first app-only bank, used feedback insights to simplify its mortgage journey and cut related customer calls by 69%. Numbers like these are why the sticker price is the wrong place to start the evaluation. Start with the cost of the problem: the analyst hours spent coding feedback by hand, the decisions delayed by weeks-long analysis cycles, and the professional services fees attached to your current stack. Thematic's ROI of CX guide covers how to put dollar figures on those. A buyer's checklist for pricing conversations Seven questions that surface the real cost before you sign: What unit is the price based on: seats, interactions, data records, or comment volume? How is the unit counted? What happens to the price at twice our current feedback volume? Ask for the number in writing. What is included in implementation, and what is billed as professional services? At what hourly rate? Can our analysts build reports and edit the theme model themselves, or does that route through your services team? Which capabilities in this demo are add-ons priced separately from the platform tier? What is the annual escalation at renewal? What overage charges apply, and is there a cap? A vendor who answers all seven crisply is telling you the real price. A vendor who cannot is telling you something too. The short answer Customer feedback analytics software costs anywhere from $19 per month for self-serve survey tools to several hundred thousand dollars per year for enterprise platforms, with the middle of the enterprise market clustering in the tens of thousands: Qualtrics deal data shows a median near $30,000 per year, and Medallia's filed government pricing listed platform tiers from $20,000 to $168,000. Thematic prices on comment volume, datasets, and support as a custom quote. Whatever the vendor, model the total cost, not the license: implementation, professional services, overages, and your own analysts' hours routinely exceed the subscription line. The fastest test: run the seven checklist questions above in your next pricing call.

title: Auction-Bound 1993 Range Rover Classic Comes with a Matching 2027 Model
summary: If you’re a Range Rover fan, the perfect two-car garage is headed to auction in less than a month. RM Sotheby’s will soon auction off a 1993 Range Rover Classic that has been fully restored by Range Rover and a matching 2027 Range Rover SV Ultra as a pair. The 1993 model is a four-door, […]
body_text: If you’re a Range Rover fan , the perfect two-car garage is headed to auction in less than a month. RM Sotheby’s will soon auction off a 1993 Range Rover Classic that has been fully restored by Range Rover and a matching 2027 Range Rover SV Ultra as a pair. The 1993 model is a four-door, short-wheelbase model that was restored and modified specifically for the auction. It’s finished in Titan Silver Metallic, a color launched on the current-generation Range Rover that’s only available on the new SV Ultra trim. We’re told that this highly reflective color features real aluminum flakes that make the body panels look almost like liquid metal. Range Rover also added newer-style lettering on the hood and the tailgate, fitted a set of 16-inch wheels finished in Satin Platinum Atlas, and removed the plastic cladding from both sides. Inside, you’ll find two-tone Orchid White and Cinder Gray Ultrafabrics upholstery, which is one of the combinations available on the 2027 SV Ultra, and a lot more leather than this SUV was originally built with. Range Rover Range Rover Range Rover Range Rover Range Rover All told, Range Rover Classic claims it spent over 2000 hours making this 33-year-old off-roader like-new. The modifications are only skin-deep, however, so power comes from a stock, 182-horsepower 3.9-liter V-8 linked to a four-speed automatic gearbox. Range Rover’s technicians rebuilt the engine, transmission, suspension, brakes, and steering to give the next owner peace of mind. The matching SV Ultra will be the first example sent to the American market. It hasn’t been built yet, but it will be pretty much identical to the model pictured in our gallery. Based on the long-wheelbase model and positioned at the top of the Range Rover family, the SUV will feature Titan Silver Metallic paint, Satin Platinum Atlas accents on the 23-inch wheels, and an Orchid White and Cinder Gray two-tone interior. It’s V-8-powered as well, though its eight-cylinder is a 4.4-liter twin-turbo sourced from BMW. The restored 1993 Range Rover Classic and the matching 2027 Range Rover SV Ultra are scheduled to cross the block as a pair on August 14, 2026, during the RM Sotheby’s The Monterey Auction 2026 . The pair is offered without a reserve, but don’t expect to bag a two-for-one deal. RM set the pre-auction estimate at between $750,000 and $950,000 excluding the buyer’s premium.
